messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: I get the impulse behind sanctuary policies, but I think it undermines basic rule of law when local police decline to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement. If someone is arrested for a serious crime and happens to be undocumented, I don't see why local jails should shield them from a detainer request. Public safety works best when different levels of law enforcement can share information rather than operate as isolated silos.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I understand that worry, but in my view the bigger public safety risk comes from immigrant communities being too afraid to call the police at all. If people think reporting a crime or even being a witness might lead to a family member being deported, they stay silent, and that makes everyone less safe, not more. Local police depend on trust from the neighborhoods they serve, and blending their role with federal immigration enforcement erodes that trust in ways that are hard to rebuild.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: That's a fair concern about trust, and I don't dismiss it, but I think there's a difference between routine policing and honoring a specific detainer tied to someone already in custody for a separate offense. Nobody is asking patrol officers to go knocking on doors asking for papers. It seems reasonable to me that once someone is already in the system, a quick handoff of information doesn't chill community reporting the way broader immigration sweeps would.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I hear that distinction, but even detainer requests sweep up people who were never convicted of anything, sometimes based on minor charges that get dropped later, and that uncertainty is exactly what makes communities wary of any entanglement between local police and federal enforcement. I also think it's worth remembering that these requests are not always honored by the agencies asked to carry them out, for all sorts of practical and legal reasons. [[CLAIM]]
